title: FAST Entry Test Syllabus and Format Explained
excerpt: A breakdown of what's actually on the FAST-NUCES Entry Test — sections, question counts, and negative marking — so you know exactly what you're preparing for.

content.text: What the FAST Entry Test actually covers

If you're aiming for a FAST-NUCES campus — Lahore, Islamabad, Karachi, Peshawar, Chiniot-Faisalabad (CFD), or the newest campus, Multan — you'll usually sit the university's own NU Entry Test rather than ECAT or NUST's NET. It's a separate exam with its own structure, and confusing it with ECAT prep is one of the more common mistakes students make going in.

The test is built around four sections: Advanced Mathematics, Basic Mathematics, Analytical/IQ Reasoning, and English. Advanced Mathematics draws on your FSc Part I and Part II syllabus and carries the largest share of the paper, currently around 50%. Basic Mathematics is lighter — arithmetic, percentages, ratios, and number sense rather than calculus-level content — at around 20%. Analytical/IQ Reasoning also sits at around 20% and is the section most students find least familiar, since it isn't taught directly in FSc at all. English is the smallest of the four sections, at around 10%, and follows an SAT-style pattern rather than the grammar-drill style you may be used to from school tests.

items: Advanced Mathematics (~50%): the heaviest-weighted section, drawn from FSc Part I & II
Analytical/IQ Reasoning (~20%): pattern recognition and logical reasoning, not FSc content
English (~10%): comprehension, sentence correction, vocabulary in an SAT-style format

content.text: The test uses negative marking, so guessing blindly on questions you have no idea about can cost you more than it gains. This changes your in-test strategy compared to a test with no penalty for wrong answers — on FAST's paper, an educated elimination of two or three options before guessing is worth it, but a pure random guess across many unknown questions usually isn't.

Exact question counts, section weightages, and negative marking values are set by FAST-NUCES and can be revised between cycles — confirm the current pattern on nu.edu.pk before you build a study plan around it. Some older guides still show a different, higher weightage for English than the ~10% reflected here — check the current official sample paper if you see conflicting numbers elsewhere.
Why the section split matters for your prep time

A lot of students default to spending most of their prep hours on Advanced Mathematics because it's the biggest section, which isn't wrong — but it means Basic Maths, English, and IQ often get treated as afterthoughts, when in fact all four sections score identically per question. A student who's strong in Advanced Maths but weak in IQ reasoning is often better off spending an extra week on IQ pattern practice than squeezing marginal gains out of an already-strong section.

This is especially true for the IQ section, since it's the one part of the test that has almost no overlap with your FSc coursework. You can't cram it the way you can cram a Maths chapter you've seen before — it needs its own dedicated practice across the pattern types that show up (number series, verbal reasoning, logical puzzles, and so on).
English deserves more respect than its size suggests

Because English is the smallest section and isn't a "core" FSc subject the way Maths or Physics is, a lot of engineering-track students treat it as the section they'll "just wing." That's still a risky assumption even at ~10% of the paper, since SAT-style English rewards specific comprehension and sentence-correction skills that aren't the same as general fluency. If your day-to-day English is strong but you've never sat a timed, SAT-style comprehension section, it's worth doing a few timed practice sets specifically to get used to the pacing — the section may be small, but it's still fast, reliable marks if you've prepared for the format.
Putting a study plan together around this structure

Once you know the section breakdown, the practical next step is figuring out where your time is best spent relative to where you're already strong. A rough starting split for most FSc students preparing over 8-10 weeks looks something like: the largest block of time on Advanced Maths since it's the biggest section, a steady weekly block on IQ reasoning since it needs the most from-scratch practice, regular but shorter timed English sets given its smaller share, and Basic Maths kept fresh with lighter, more occasional review since it tends to need less total time to solidify.

items: Advanced Mathematics: the largest weekly time block, focused on FSc Part I & II topics
Analytical/IQ Reasoning: consistent practice every week, since it can't be crammed late
English: shorter, regular timed sets in an SAT-style format, not just casual reading
Basic Mathematics: lighter, periodic review rather than daily drilling

content.text: The section names and rough weightage give you the map, but the real preparation work is in past-paper practice under timed conditions, which tells you far more about your actual readiness than reading the syllabus ever will. You can track how your accuracy is trending across each of these four sections separately using PrepXMentor's per-topic breakdown, so you're not relying on a single overall score to guess where you're actually improving.

items.question: What sections are on the FAST Entry Test?
items.answer: Four sections: Advanced Mathematics (~50%), Basic Mathematics (~20%), Analytical/IQ Reasoning (~20%), and English (~10%). Advanced Math carries the largest share of the paper.

items.question: Does the FAST Entry Test have negative marking?
items.answer: Yes. Wrong answers are penalized, so a pure random guess across unfamiliar questions is usually a bad trade — educated elimination of one or two options before guessing tends to be worth it, blind guessing generally isn't.

items.question: How much of the FAST Entry Test is English?
items.answer: Around 10% — the smallest of the four sections. It's still worth dedicated timed practice, since the SAT-style format rewards specific skills that general fluency alone doesn't cover.

items.question: Which section should I prioritize if I'm short on prep time?
items.answer: Advanced Math first, since it carries the largest weight and the most content. IQ Reasoning deserves consistent weekly practice too, since it can't be crammed late — it has almost no overlap with FSc coursework.

items.question: Do all four sections count equally toward my score?
items.answer: Each question scores the same regardless of section, but the sections carry different overall weights (50/20/20/10), so a weak section with a bigger weight — typically Advanced Math or IQ — costs you more than a weak section with a smaller one.
